cues.text: Chapter six is the Lagos Smart City case.
This is a teaching scenario, so let's work through it carefully.
The scenario describes a smart-city transformation in Lagos.
In it, agency data sits in silos, meaning each agency keeps its own data separate from the others.
Reporting is done manually.
Response to problems is slow.
And there are risks of fraud and risks to privacy.
Those are the problems the scenario sets up.
To address them, the source proposes a polyglot architecture.
Polyglot means using more than one kind of database or data technology, each for the job it suits best.
Here, four components are named.
First, AI is used for traffic prediction and for predicting service demand.
Second, a permissioned ledger is used to record the provenance of transactions between agencies.
Provenance means a trustworthy record of where something came from and how it moved.
Permissioned means only approved participants can take part in the ledger.
Third, a graph database represents roads, services, resources, and the relationships between them.
A graph suits this because roads connect to other roads, and services and resources sit in particular places.
Fourth, relational databases hold the authoritative transactional records.
Authoritative means these are the trusted, official records.
Now the example in the source, step by step.
Sensors send traffic events.
Then edge processing aggregates local congestion.
Edge processing means the data is processed close to where it is produced, near the sensors, and combined into a summary of local congestion before it travels further.
Next, AI estimates demand.
A graph represents road connectivity and the locations of emergency services.
And signed ledger entries record approved inter-agency data exchanges.
Signed means each entry carries a digital signature, so it can be attributed to whoever approved it.
Note that these entries record exchanges that were approved.
The source then gives an important caution.
Do not place raw citizen health data or identity data on the chain.
The ledger should hold records about exchanges, not sensitive personal data itself.
The source also lists what must be implemented: access controls, minimisation, lawful sharing, auditability, reliability, and evaluation.
Access controls limit who can see or change data.
Minimisation means collecting and sharing only what is needed.
Lawful sharing means data moves between agencies only where the law allows.
Auditability means actions can be reviewed afterwards.
Reliability means the system keeps working dependably.
And evaluation means you measure whether the system actually performs as intended.
Finally, a limitation that the source states plainly.
This is a scenario analysis.
It is not evidence that the described systems were deployed.
So treat it as a way of reasoning about how these database technologies could fit together, and not as a report of something that was actually built in Lagos.
